MENINGES_DURA_ARACHNOID_PIA.name: Meninges (Dura mater, Arachnoid membrane and Pia mater)
MENINGES_DURA_ARACHNOID_PIA.summary: Three concentric membranes that cover and protect the central nervous system: (1) Dura mater (the outer fibrous pachymeninge, comprising the falx cerebri in the interhemispheric fissure and the tentorium cerebelli), (2) Trabecular arachnoid membrane in the subarachnoid space filled with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and Pacchioni’s arachnoid granulations adjacent to the superior sagittal sinus, and (3) the inner vascular pia mater, which adheres to the cortical gyri and sulci.
MENINGES_DURA_ARACHNOID_PIA.clinical: Bacterial or viral meningitis (neck stiffness, Kernig’s and Brudzinski’s signs), epidural haematoma (rupture of the middle meningeal artery), subdural haematoma (rupture of cortical bridging veins) and subarachnoid haemorrhage.
functions: Mechanical protection against traumatic brain injury and cranial compartmentalisation (cerebral falx and cerebellar tentorium)
Hydrostatic support of the floating brain in the subarachnoid fluid (reducing the effective weight from 1,400 g to ~50 g)
Unidirectional reabsorption of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) by Pacchioni’s arachnoid granulations into the superior sagittal sinus
Haemato-leukorrheic barrier and perivascular pial lining (Virchow-Robin spaces / Glymphatic system)

FRONTAL_LOBE.name: Frontal Lobe
FRONTAL_LOBE.summary: The seat of higher executive functions, planning, inhibitory control (dorsolateral and orbitofrontal prefrontal cortex), somatotopic voluntary motor control (precentral gyrus / Penfield’s motor homunculus) and the motor expression of speech (Broca’s area).
FRONTAL_LOBE.clinical: Broca’s motor aphasia (non-fluent speech with preserved comprehension), contralateral hemiparesis/hemiplegia, executive dysfunction syndrome or frontal apathy/disinhibition (Phineas Gage syndrome) and frontotemporal dementia.
functions: Contralateral voluntary motor execution via the corticospinal tract (Area 4)
Complex motor planning, bimanual coordination and binocular vision (Areas 6 and 8)
Working memory, abstraction, ethical judgement and the regulation of social behaviour (Areas 9–12)
Phonological and syntactic organisation of spoken and written language (Broca’s area — 44 and 45)

PARIETAL_LOBE.name: Parietal Lobe
PARIETAL_LOBE.summary: Primary centre for somatosensory integration (epicritic touch, conscious proprioception, pain and temperature in the post-central gyrus), visuospatial perception, body schema and symbolic calculation.
PARIETAL_LOBE.clinical: Contralateral spatial hemineglect (right parietal lobe lesion), astereognosia, ideomotor apraxia and Gerstmann’s syndrome (digital agnosia, acalculia, agraphia and right-left disorientation in the dominant angular gyrus).
functions: Primary sensory somatotopy in the post-central gyrus (sensory homunculus — areas 3, 1 and 2)
Stereognosis (tactile recognition of objects) and graphesthesia in the superior parietal lobe
Multimodal semantic integration, reading and calculation in the supramarginal (40) and angular (39) gyri
Three-dimensional spatial attention and egocentric/allocentric maps of peripersonal space

TEMPORAL_LOBE.name: Time Wolf
TEMPORAL_LOBE.summary: It processes primary auditory processing (Heschl’s transverse gyri), semantic comprehension of language (Wernicke’s area), visual face recognition (fusiform gyrus) and houses the hippocampal-amygdala complex on its medial surface.
TEMPORAL_LOBE.clinical: Wernicke’s sensory aphasia (fluent but paraphasic/neologistic speech and lack of comprehension), prosopagnosia (inability to recognise faces) and temporal lobe epilepsy with olfactory auras/déjà vu.
functions: Primary and secondary auditory tonotopy in Heschl’s gyri (Areas 41 and 42)
Phonemic decoding and language comprehension in Wernicke’s area (posterior Area 22)
Ventral visual pathway (“What?”): object and face recognition in the Fusiform Gyrus (Area 37)
Auditory-limbic integration and the consolidation of long-term semantic memories

OCCIPITAL_LOBE.name: Occipital Lobe
OCCIPITAL_LOBE.summary: Entirely dedicated to vision, it receives optical signals from the lateral geniculate body at the edges of the calcarine sulcus (V1 / Area 17 — Gennari’s stria) and distributes them to the associative areas V2–V5.
OCCIPITAL_LOBE.clinical: Contralateral homonymous hemianopsia with macular preservation (posterior cerebral artery occlusion), cortical blindness with Anton’s syndrome (denial of blindness and visual confabulation) and central achromatopsia.
functions: Point-to-point retinotopic mapping in the Primary Visual Cortex (V1 / Area 17)
Decomposition of edge orientation, binocular contrast, depth disparity and colour (V2/V4)
Perception of movement and optical speed (V5 / MT area)
Origin of the visual pathways: Dorsal (Parietal — ‘Where/How to act’) and Ventral (Temporal — ‘What it is’)

INSULAR_CORTEX.name: Insular Cortex (Reil’s Insula)
INSULAR_CORTEX.summary: The fifth hidden cerebral lobe, situated at the base of the Sylvian lateral sulcus, is responsible for conscious interoception (perception of the heartbeat, breathing, visceral pain and hunger), primary gustation and affective empathy.
INSULAR_CORTEX.clinical: Neurogenic arrhythmias and T-wave inversion following a right insular stroke, sudden loss of the fissure due to nicotine/substance dependence following insular damage, and alterations in pain perception (assymbolia for pain).
functions: Conscious visceral interoceptive map (the body’s internal physiological state)
Primary gustatory cortex and olfactory-gustatory integration of taste
Processing the affective matrix of pain, risk aversion, disgust and emotional empathy
Cardiovascular autonomic control (sympathetic/parasympathetic modulation of heart rate)

CEREBELLUM.name: Cerebellum (Folia, Vermis & Hemispheres)
CEREBELLUM.summary: It contains more than half of all the neurons in the human brain (~69 billion), organised into thin horizontal layers (folia) and Purkinje cells, which compare cortical motor intent with proprioceptive feedback in real time.
CEREBELLUM.clinical: Ipsilateral Cerebellar Syndrome: gait ataxia (widened base), dysmetria (index-to-nose test), dysdiadochokinesia, intention tremor, scandia dysarthria and nystagmus.
functions: Fine coordination of muscle strength, range of motion and timing (metria and diadocokinesia)
Maintenance of axial balance and the vestibulo-ocular reflex (flocculonodular lobe and vermis)
Instantaneous correction of motor errors via climbing fibres from the inferior olive to Purkinje cells
Procedural motor learning and the automation of cognitive-motor skills

CORPUS_CALLOSUM.name: Corpus Callosum
CORPUS_CALLOSUM.summary: The largest white matter structure in the nervous system (~200 million myelinated axons), connecting the left and right cerebral hemispheres both homotopically and heterotopically.
CORPUS_CALLOSUM.clinical: Interhemispheric Disconnection Syndrome (Split-Brain Syndrome), Alien Hand Syndrome, alexia without agraphia (lesion of the splenium and left occipital cortex) and agenesis of the corpus callosum.
functions: Ultra-rapid interhemispheric transfer of sensory, motor and linguistic information
Unification of the left and right visual fields via the splenium of the corpus callosum
Synchronised bilateral motor coordination via the knee and corpus callosum
Integration of emotional prosody (right hemisphere) with verbal syntax (left hemisphere)

THALAMUS.name: Thalamus (Dorsal Diencephalon)
THALAMUS.summary: A mandatory relay and filtering station for all conscious sensory pathways (except smell), as well as integrating the motor circuits of the basal ganglia and the cerebellum with the cortex.
THALAMUS.clinical: Dejerine-Roussy thalamic pain syndrome (hemi-hypoaesthesia followed by excruciating contralateral allodynic neuropathic pain following a posterolateral thalamic stroke) and fatal familial insomnia.
functions: Somatoseptive relay of the body (VPL nucleus) and the face/trigeminal nerve (VPM nucleus)
Visual (Lateral Geniculate Body — LGB) and auditory (Medial Geniculate Body — MGB) relay
Modulation of motor loops in the basal ganglia and cerebellum (anterior ventral and lateral ventral nuclei)
Regulation of the sleep-wake cycle and alpha/spindle rhythms by the thalamic reticular nucleus

HYPOTHALAMUS.name: Hypothalamus & Pituitary Axis
HYPOTHALAMUS.summary: The supreme regulator of the body’s homeostasis and the autonomic nervous system, linked to the pituitary gland to translate neural signals into systemic hormonal control.
HYPOTHALAMUS.clinical: Central diabetes insipidus (ADH deficiency), syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion (SIADH), narcolepsy (loss of orexinergic neurons) and severe thermoregulatory disorders.
functions: Thermoregulation (the anterior hypothalamus dissipates heat; the posterior hypothalamus retains heat)
Endogenous 24-hour circadian pacemaker in the suprachiasmatic nucleus
Regulation of thirst/osmolarity, hunger/satiety (Arcuate, Ventromedial and Lateral Nuclei)
Synthesis of Oxytocin and ADH (Vasopressin) in the Supraoptic and Paraventricular Nuclei and Control by the Anterior Pituitary

HIPPOCAMPUS.name: Hippocampus & Fornix
HIPPOCAMPUS.summary: The medial temporal archicortex is essential for the consolidation of declarative memory (episodic and semantic) and for cognitive spatial mapping (place cells).
HIPPOCAMPUS.clinical: Severe anterograde amnesia (the inability to form new declarative memories, as in the classic case of patient H.M.), early hippocampal atrophy in Alzheimer’s disease and mesial temporal sclerosis.
functions: Synaptic consolidation of short-term memories into long-term memories via Long-Term Potentiation (LTP)
Hippocampal Trisynaptic Circuit (Entorhinal Cortex → Dentate Gyrus → CA3 → CA1 → Subiculum → Fornix)
Spatial navigation and geographical orientation via place cells (hippocampus) and grid cells (entorhinal cortex)
Continuous adult neurogenesis in the subgranular zone of the dentate gyrus

AMYGDALA.name: Cerebral Amygdala (Amygdala Complex)
AMYGDALA.summary: An emotional sentinel of the limbic system situated in the anterior temporal pole, which assigns an immediate affective valence to sensory stimuli and triggers the autonomic ‘fight-or-flight’ response.
AMYGDALA.clinical: Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD), anxiety/panic disorders (amygdala hyper-reactivity with prefrontal hypofunction) and Klüver-Bucy syndrome (placidity, hyperorality and absence of fear following bilateral lesion).
functions: Fear conditioning and ultra-rapid detection of environmental threats (via the thalamic-amygdala pathway)
Emotional modulation of memory consolidation in the hippocampus (emotionally intense memories)
Sympathetic and neuroendocrine autonomic activation (HPA axis / cortisol) via the central nucleus of the amygdala
Recognition of facial expressions of fear, anger and social trustworthiness

BASAL_GANGLIA.name: Basal Ganglia (Striatum & Globus Pallidus)
BASAL_GANGLIA.badge: SELECTION OF ACTUATORS & MOTOR CONTROL SYSTEMS
BASAL_GANGLIA.summary: A complex of deep subcortical nuclei that operate within cortico-striato-pallido-thalamic-cortical loops (the facilitatory direct pathway and the inhibitory indirect pathway) to initiate desired movements and suppress unwanted movements.
BASAL_GANGLIA.clinical: Parkinson’s disease (dopaminergic degeneration of the substantia nigra → bradykinesia, cogwheel rigidity and resting tremor), Huntington’s chorea and hemiballism (lesion of the subthalamic nucleus of Luys).
functions: Direct Pathway (D1 Receptors): disinhibits the thalamus and facilitates the smooth initiation of voluntary movements
Indirect pathway (D2 receptors): inhibits the thalamus to suppress unwanted involuntary movements
Nigrostriatal dopaminergic modulation originating in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNpc)
Reinforcement learning, habit formation and motivation (Ventral Striatum / Nucleus Accumbens)

MIDBRAIN.name: Midbrain (Upper Brain Stem)
MIDBRAIN.summary: Upper segment of the brainstem, through which the Aqueduct of Sylvius passes, containing the cerebral peduncles, the superior and inferior colliculi, the red nucleus, the substantia nigra and the ventral tegmental area (VTA).
MIDBRAIN.clinical: Weber’s syndrome (contralateral hemiplegia + ipsilateral third cranial nerve palsy with ptosis and mydriasis), Parinaud’s syndrome (paralysis of the superior vertical conjugate eye movement) and decerebrate rigidity.
functions: Reflexive head and eye movements in response to visual stimuli (superior colliculi) and auditory stimuli (inferior colliculi)
Origin of the oculomotor nerve (CN III — ocular motility and the Edinger-Westphal pupillary photomotor reflex) and the trochlear nerve (CN IV)
Dopamine production in the substantia nigra (nigroestriatal pathway) and in the VTA (mesolimbic and mesocortical pathways)
Descending endogenous analgesia via the periaqueductal grey matter (PAG)

PONS.name: Varólio’s Bridge (Annular Protrusion)
PONS.summary: A ventral prominence of the brainstem situated between the midbrain and the medulla oblongata, serving as a major bridge of transverse fibres between the cerebral cortex and the cerebellum and housing the nuclei of cranial nerves V, VI, VII and VIII.
PONS.clinical: Locked-in Syndrome (ventral infarction of the pontine base due to basilar occlusion -> tetraplegia and anarthria with intact consciousness and preserved vertical eye movements) and Central Pontine Myelinolysis.
functions: Massive relaying of cortical commands to the cerebellum via the pontine nuclei and the middle cerebellar peduncle
Pneumotaxic and apnoeic centres (fine-tuning of the transition from inhalation to exhalation)
The trigeminal (CN V), abducens (CN VI), facial (CN VII) and vestibulocochlear (CN VIII) nerve nuclei
The main source of noradrenaline for the entire brain is the locus coeruleus (alertness and attention)

MEDULLA_OBLONGATA.name: Medulla Oblongata
MEDULLA_OBLONGATA.summary: The caudal segment of the brainstem, which continues into the spinal cord at the foramen magnum, containing the decussation of the pyramids (the motor crossing of 85 per cent of the corticospinal fibres) and the vital autonomic centres.
MEDULLA_OBLONGATA.clinical: Wallenberg’s lateral bulbar syndrome (occlusion of the PICA -> dysphagia, hoarseness, ipsilateral Horner’s syndrome, vertigo and cross-sided loss of temperature and pain sensation) and cardiorespiratory arrest in tonsillar herniation.
functions: Automatic control of respiratory rhythm generation (Dorsal and Ventral Respiratory Groups / Pre-Bötzinger Complex)
Beat-by-beat regulation of blood pressure and heart rate (Solitary Tract Nucleus and Rostroventrolateral Bulb)
Motor decussation of the pyramids (lateral corticospinal tract) and sensory decussation of the medial lemniscus (gracile and cuneiform)
Nuclei of the glossopharyngeal (IX), vagus (X), accessory (XI) and hypoglossal (XII) nerves — swallowing, phonation, coughing and vomiting

SPINAL_CORD.name: Spinal Cord, Conus Medullaris & Cauda Equina
SPINAL_CORD.badge: SPINAL NERVOUS SYSTEM • MOTOR AND SENSORY TRACKS
SPINAL_CORD.summary: The cylindrical axis of the central nervous system, protected by the spinal canal, showing the medullary H of grey matter (dorsal sensory, intermediate autonomic and ventral motor horns) surrounded by the white matter tracts and terminating at the medullary cone (L1/L2) and the cauda equina.
SPINAL_CORD.clinical: Brown-Séquard spinal hemisection syndrome (ipsilateral paralysis and loss of proprioception + contralateral loss of thermal and pain sensation), cauda equina syndrome (saddle anaesthesia and urinary retention) and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).
functions: Descending motor conduction via the lateral/anterior corticospinal, rubrospinal, reticulospinal and vestibulospinal tracts
Ascending sensory transmission via the dorsal columns (gracile/cuneiform: epicritic touch and proprioception) and the spinothalamic tract (pain and temperature)
Integration of spinal reflex arcs (patellar/Achilles myotatic reflex and flexor withdrawal reflex)
Origin of the thoracolumbar sympathetic (T1–L2) and sacral parasympathetic (S2–S4) columns and of the cauda equina roots

OLFACTORY_NERVE_CN1.name: Olfactory Nerve (I Cranial Nerve)
OLFACTORY_NERVE_CN1.badge: CRANIAL NERVE I • SMELL SIGNALS GO DIRECTLY TO THE CORTEX
OLFACTORY_NERVE_CN1.summary: The first cranial nerve pair, which is purely special sensory (Special Visceral Afferent), and is the only human sensory pathway that reaches the primary olfactory cortex (piriform cortex and amygdala) directly, without first passing through the thalamus.
OLFACTORY_NERVE_CN1.clinical: Post-traumatic anosmia or hyposmia (fracture of the cribriform plate with cerebrospinal fluid fistula / CSF rhinorrhoea), early prodromal hyposmia in Parkinson’s disease and Foster-Kennedy syndrome.
functions: Chemical transduction of odour molecules by the cilia of bipolar neurons in the superior olfactory mucosa
The passage of the olfactory filaments through the foramina of the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone to the glomeruli of the olfactory bulb
Direct connection to the piriform cortex, amygdala and entorhinal cortex (instant evocation of emotional memories through smell)

OPTIC_NERVE_CN2.name: Optic Nerve, Chiasm & Optic Tract (Pair II)
OPTIC_NERVE_CN2.summary: It is formed by the axons of the retinal ganglion cells (myelinated by oligodendrocytes, constituting a true tract of the diencephalon), whose nasal fibres cross at the optic chiasm on their way to the lateral geniculate body.
OPTIC_NERVE_CN2.clinical: Retrobulbar optic neuritis (often the initial manifestation of multiple sclerosis, with Marcus Gunn’s relative afferent pupillary defect), heteronymous bitemporal hemianopsia (compression of the optic chiasm by a pituitary adenoma) and papilloedema.
functions: High-resolution imaging of the foveal (macula) and peripheral retina
Crossing of the fibres from the nasal hemiretina at the optic chiasm (combining the left and right visual hemifields)
Assessment of the direct and consensual pupillary photomotor reflexes towards the mesencephalic pre-tectal area

OCULOMOTOR_NERVES_CN3_4_6.name: Oculomotor (III), Trochlear (IV) & Abducens (VI) Nerves
OCULOMOTOR_NERVES_CN3_4_6.badge: III, IV & VI PAIRS • EXTRINSIC AND INTRINSIC OCULAR MOTOR FUNCTION
OCULOMOTOR_NERVES_CN3_4_6.summary: A trio of motor cranial nerves that pass through the cavernous sinus and the superior orbital fissure to control, with micrometric precision, the six extraocular muscles, the levator palpebrae superioris and the pupillary sphincter.
OCULOMOTOR_NERVES_CN3_4_6.clinical: Paralysis of the third cranial nerve (eyes deviating outwards and downwards, ptosis and fixed mydriasis due to an aneurysm of the posterior communicating artery), vertical diplopia when descending stairs (lesion of the fourth cranial nerve) and convergent strabismus (lesion of the sixth cranial nerve).
functions: CN III (Oculomotor): innervates the superior rectus, inferior rectus, medial rectus, inferior oblique, levator palpebrae superioris and pupillary miosis (Edinger-Westphal)
CN IV (Troclear): the only nerve that emerges from the dorsal surface of the trunk, innervating the superior oblique muscle (intorsion and depression of the eye)
CN VI (Abducens): innervates the lateral rectus muscle, causing horizontal abduction of the eyeball

TRIGEMINAL_NERVE_CN5.name: Trigeminal Nerve (V Par: Branches V1, V2 and V3)
TRIGEMINAL_NERVE_CN5.badge: CRANIAL NERVE V • FACIAL SENSATION AND CHEWING
TRIGEMINAL_NERVE_CN5.summary: The largest of the cranial nerves, emerging from the anterolateral surface of the pons and branching out from the trigeminal ganglion (Gasser’s semilunar ganglion) into three major branches: Ophthalmic (V1), Maxillary (V2) and Mandibular (V3).
TRIGEMINAL_NERVE_CN5.clinical: Trigeminal Neuralgia (paroxysms of excruciating, electric-shock-like pain in the V2/V3 territories, frequently due to neurovascular compression by the superior cerebellar artery), the pathophysiology of migraine (trigeminal-vascular system) and ophthalmic herpes zoster.
functions: Tactile, thermal and pain sensitivity affecting the entire face, cornea, paranasal sinuses, teeth, anterior two-thirds of the tongue and dura mater
Branchial motor innervation (branch V3) of the masticatory muscles (masseter, temporal, medial and lateral pterygoid)
Testing of the corneopalpebral reflex (V1) and the mentonian/masseteric reflex (V3)

FACIAL_VESTIBULOCOCHLEAR_CN7_8.name: Facial (VII) & Vestibulocochlear (VIII) Nerves
FACIAL_VESTIBULOCOCHLEAR_CN7_8.badge: VII & VIII PAIRS • FACIAL EXPRESSIONS, HEARING & BALANCE
FACIAL_VESTIBULOCOCHLEAR_CN7_8.summary: They emerge together at the pontocerebellar angle and enter the internal auditory meatus: the seventh pair controls facial expressions, tearing, salivation and the anterior sense of taste; the eighth pair is responsible for hearing (cochlea) and balance (vestibular labyrinth).
FACIAL_VESTIBULOCOCHLEAR_CN7_8.clinical: Bell’s Palsy (affecting the upper and lower thirds of the ipsilateral side of the face, with Bell’s sign), Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV), Ménière’s disease and vestibular schwannoma.
functions: CN VII (Facial): motor function of all the facial expression muscles, taste sensation in the anterior two-thirds of the tongue (chorda tympani) and the lacrimal, submandibular and sublingual glands
CN VIII (Cochlear Division): sound transduction from the organ of Corti to the cochlear nuclei
CN VIII (Vestibular Division): detection of angular acceleration (semicircular canals) and linear acceleration (utricle and saccule)

VAGUS_NERVE_CN10.name: Vagus Nerve (Xth Pair) & Parasympathetic System
VAGUS_NERVE_CN10.badge: CRANIAL NERVE X • THORACOABDOMINAL PARASYMPATHETIC NERVE
VAGUS_NERVE_CN10.summary: The cranial nerve with the longest course, descending through the neck (carotid sheath), mediastinum and oesophageal hiatus to supply ~75 per cent of all parasympathetic fibres in the human body to the transverse colon.
VAGUS_NERVE_CN10.clinical: Hoarseness/dysphonia due to vocal fold paralysis (recurrent laryngeal nerve injury), vasovagal syncope, diabetic gastroparesis and vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) for refractory epilepsy and treatment-resistant depression.
functions: Reduction in heart rate (negative chronotropic effect on the sinoatrial node) and physiological bronchoconstriction
Stimulation of gastrointestinal peristalsis, gastric acid secretion, and biliary and pancreatic secretion (Gut-Brain Axis)
Motor innervation of the larynx (recurrent laryngeal nerve — phonation) and the soft palate, as well as the baroreceptor reflex
Cholinergic anti-inflammatory pathway (vagal modulation of the systemic immune response)

GLOSSOPHARYNGEAL_ACCESSORY_HYPOGLOSSAL_C.name: Glossopharyngeal (IX), Accessory (XI) & Hypoglossal (XII) Nerves
GLOSSOPHARYNGEAL_ACCESSORY_HYPOGLOSSAL_C.badge: IX, XI & XII PAIRS • SWALLOWING, SPEECH ARTICULATION AND THE NECK
GLOSSOPHARYNGEAL_ACCESSORY_HYPOGLOSSAL_C.summary: Inferior cranial nerves that control sensation in the pharynx and carotid sinus (IX), cervical rotation and shoulder elevation (XI), and the intrinsic and extrinsic motor functions of the tongue (XII).
GLOSSOPHARYNGEAL_ACCESSORY_HYPOGLOSSAL_C.clinical: Glossopharyngeal neuralgia, jugular foramen syndrome (Vernet — cranial nerves IX, X and XI), shoulder drop due to injury to cranial nerve XI, and deviation of the tongue towards the side of the lesion with atrophy and fasciculations in cases of injury to cranial nerve XII.
functions: CN IX (Glossopharyngeal): taste and sensation in the posterior third of the tongue, gag reflex, parotid gland and chemoreceptors and baroreceptors of the carotid sinus
CN XI (Spinal Accessory Nerve): motor innervation of the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles
CN XII (hypoglossal nerve): motor control of all the muscles of the tongue (genioglossus, hypoglossus, styloglossus)

CERVICAL_PLEXUS_PHRENIC.name: Cervical Plexus & Phrenic Nerve (C1–C5)
CERVICAL_PLEXUS_PHRENIC.badge: CERVICAL SNP • INNERVATION OF THE DIAPHRAGM
CERVICAL_PLEXUS_PHRENIC.summary: Composed of the ventral branches of C1 to C4 (with a contribution from C5), it gives rise to the cervical plexus for the infrahyoid muscles and the vital phrenic nerve (C3, C4, C5), which is solely responsible for the contraction of the diaphragm.
CERVICAL_PLEXUS_PHRENIC.clinical: Diaphragmatic paralysis with paradoxical elevation of the diaphragmatic hemidome (phrenic nerve injury) or mechanical respiratory arrest in high cervical spinal cord injury (above C3).
functions: Rhythmic and voluntary control of the diaphragm by the phrenic nerve (“C3, C4, C5 keep the diaphragm alive”)
Skin sensitivity of the occipital scalp, auricle, anterior neck and supraclavicular region
Referred pain from the pericardium, mediastinal pleura and subdiaphragmatic peritoneum (referred pain in the shoulder — Kehr’s sign)

BRACHIAL_PLEXUS.name: Brachial Plexus (C5–T1 Roots, Trunks & Fascicles)
BRACHIAL_PLEXUS.summary: A complex anastomotic network formed by the anterior branches from C5 to T1, which passes through the interscalene gap and divides into trunks (superior, middle, inferior), Divisions and Fascicles (Lateral, Medial and Posterior) to innervate the entire upper limb.
BRACHIAL_PLEXUS.clinical: Erb-Duchenne palsy (C5–C6 injury → ‘waiter’s tip’ posture), Klumpke’s palsy (C8–T1 lesion → claw hand + Horner’s syndrome) and thoracic outlet syndrome.
functions: Upper Trunk (C5–C6): shoulder abduction (axillary nerve / deltoid muscle) and elbow flexion (musculocutaneous nerve / biceps)
Posterior branch: extension of the entire upper limb via the radial nerve
Lateral and Medial Branches: flexor and fine intrinsic motor functions of the hand via the median and ulnar nerves

MEDIAN_ULNAR_RADIAL_NERVES.name: Median, Ulnar and Radial Nerves (Arm, Forearm and Hand)
MEDIAN_ULNAR_RADIAL_NERVES.badge: BRACHIAL SNP • FINE MOTOR SKILLS OF THE HAND
MEDIAN_ULNAR_RADIAL_NERVES.summary: A triad of major terminal nerves of the brachial plexus that run through the arm, elbow, forearm and wrist (carpal tunnel and Guyon’s canal) to control grasping, fine pincer movements and extension of the fingers.
MEDIAN_ULNAR_RADIAL_NERVES.clinical: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome / Monkey Hand (median nerve injury), Ulnar Claw Hand (Froment’s sign in ulnar nerve injury) and Wrist Drop (radial nerve injury in the spiral groove of the humerus).
functions: Median Nerve (C5–T1): pronation of the forearm, thumb opposition (thenar eminence) and palmar sensation in the 1st to 3rd fingers
Ulnar nerve (C8–T1): intrinsic muscles of the hand (interosseous muscles, adductor pollicis and hypothenar muscles) and sensation in the fifth finger
Radial nerve (C5–T1): extension of the elbow (triceps), wrist and fingers (posterior compartment)

INTERCOSTAL_SYMPATHETIC_CHAIN.name: Intercostal Nerves (T1–T12) & Thoracolumbar Sympathetic Chain
INTERCOSTAL_SYMPATHETIC_CHAIN.summary: The set of 12 pairs of segmental thoracic nerves (dermatomes T1–T12) associated with the paravertebral ganglia of the sympathetic trunk, which orchestrate the systemic adrenergic response.
INTERCOSTAL_SYMPATHETIC_CHAIN.clinical: Postherpetic neuralgia (reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus in a thoracic dorsal root ganglion), Horner’s syndrome (T1 sympathetic lesion / stellate ganglion) and primary hyperhidrosis.
functions: Motor innervation of the internal and external intercostal muscles in thoracic ventilatory mechanics
Exteroceptive sensitivity in the thoracic dermatomes and abdominal wall (T4 = nipple; T10 = umbilical scar)
Sympathetic chain: bronchodilation, tachycardia, splanchnic vasoconstriction, piloerection and sweating (splanchnic nerves)

LUMBOSACRAL_PLEXUS.name: Lumbosacral Plexus & Femoral Nerve (L1–S4)
LUMBOSACRAL_PLEXUS.badge: SNP LOMBOSSACRAL • PELVIS AND ANTERIOR THIGH
LUMBOSACRAL_PLEXUS.summary: Anatomical and functional union of the lumbar (L1–L4, within the psoas major muscle) and sacral (L4–S4, in the posterior pelvic wall) plexuses, giving rise to the femoral, obturator, pudendal and sciatic nerves.
LUMBOSACRAL_PLEXUS.clinical: Femoral neuropathy (weakness when climbing stairs or standing up from a chair, loss of the patellar reflex and hypoaesthesia in the distribution of the saphenous nerve) and meralgia paraesthetica (compression of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve).
functions: Femoral nerve (L2–L4): hip flexion (iliopsoas), powerful knee extension (quadriceps femoris) and patellar reflex (L4)
Obturator nerve (L2–L4): adduction of the thigh and sensation in the medial aspect of the thigh
Sacral Plexus and Pudendal Nerve (S2–S4): urinary and faecal continence and perineal sensation

SCIATIC_TIBIAL_FIBULAR_NERVES.name: Sciatic (Ischiatic), Tibial and Common Peroneal Nerves (L4–S3)
SCIATIC_TIBIAL_FIBULAR_NERVES.badge: LARGEST NERVE IN THE HUMAN BODY • LOWER LIMB
SCIATIC_TIBIAL_FIBULAR_NERVES.summary: The longest and thickest nerve in the human body (roots L4–S3), emerging through the greater sciatic foramen below the piriformis muscle and dividing in the popliteal fossa into the tibial and common peroneal nerves, which extend down to the foot.
SCIATIC_TIBIAL_FIBULAR_NERVES.clinical: Sciatica / L5–S1 radiculopathy due to a lumbar disc herniation (positive Lasègue’s sign), piriformis syndrome and foot drop / shuffling gait (injury to the common peroneal nerve at the neck of the fibula).
functions: Sciatic trunk: knee flexion by the hamstring muscles (biceps femoris, semitendinosus and semimembranosus)
Tibial nerve (L4–S3): plantar flexion of the foot (gastrocnemius and soleus), Achilles reflex (S1) and sensation in the sole of the foot
Common Peroneal Nerve (L4–S2): dorsiflexion of the ankle (anterior tibial), eversion of the foot and extension of the toes

INTERNAL_CAROTID_ARTERIES.name: Internal Carotid Arteries (Anterior Circulation)
INTERNAL_CAROTID_ARTERIES.badge: VASCULAR • 80 PER CENT OF CEREBRAL BLOOD FLOW
INTERNAL_CAROTID_ARTERIES.summary: The main arterial trunks of the anterior cerebral circulation, entering the base of the skull via the carotid canal, passing through the cavernous sinus (carotid siphon) and branching into the anterior and middle cerebral arteries.
INTERNAL_CAROTID_ARTERIES.clinical: Atherosclerotic carotid stenosis with ipsilateral transient blindness (embolism to the central retinal artery) and haemispheric ischaemic stroke, carotid dissection (neck pain + Horner’s syndrome) and paraclinoid aneurysms.
functions: Supplies approximately 80 per cent of the total cerebral blood flow (approximately 750 mL/min at rest)
Branches of the ophthalmic artery (supplying the retina and optic nerve) and the anterior choroidal artery (supplying the inner capsule and hippocampus)
Connection to the posterior circulation via the posterior communicating artery

VERTEBRAL_BASILAR_ARTERIES.name: Vertebral Arteries & Basilar Artery (Posterior Circulation)
VERTEBRAL_BASILAR_ARTERIES.badge: VASCULAR • BLOOD SUPPLY TO THE TRUNK AND CEREBELLUM
VERTEBRAL_BASILAR_ARTERIES.summary: The two vertebral arteries ascend through the transverse foramina from C6 to C1, pass through the foramen magnum and join at the bulbopontine junction to form the basilar artery over the basilar groove of the pons.
VERTEBRAL_BASILAR_ARTERIES.clinical: Vertebrobasilar insufficiency (vertigo, diplopia, dysarthria, ataxia and drop attacks) and basilar artery thrombosis (a devastating neurological emergency leading to locked-in syndrome).
functions: Vital blood supply to the medulla oblongata, pons, midbrain, cerebellum (PICA, AICA and ACS), posterior thalamus and occipital lobe
Origin of the Anterior Spinal Artery and the Posterior Inferior Cerebellar Arteries (PICA)
Terminal bifurcation of the basilar artery into the two posterior cerebral arteries (PCA)

CIRCLE_OF_WILLIS.name: Willis’s Polygon (Circular Artery System of the Brain)
CIRCLE_OF_WILLIS.badge: COLATERAL ANASTOMOSIS AT THE BASE OF THE SKULL
CIRCLE_OF_WILLIS.summary: A heptagonal anastomotic arterial ring situated in the interpeduncular cistern around the optic chiasm and pituitary infundibulum, connecting the carotid (anterior) and vertebrobasilar (posterior) circulations.
CIRCLE_OF_WILLIS.clinical: The site of 85 per cent of intracranial saccular aneurysms (particularly in the anterior and posterior communicating arteries), the rupture of which causes subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH — ‘the worst headache of your life’).
functions: Immediate collateral redistribution of blood flow in the event of occlusion of a carotid or vertebral artery
Haemodynamic equalisation of cerebral perfusion pressure between the two hemispheres
Origin of the central perforating arteries (lenticuloestriate and thalamoperforating) to the diencephalon and internal capsule

MIDDLE_CEREBRAL_ARTERY.name: Middle Cerebral Artery (MCA), Anterior Cerebral Artery (ACA) & Posterior Cerebral Artery (PCA)
MIDDLE_CEREBRAL_ARTERY.summary: The three major pairs of cerebral arteries that supply the entire telencephalic cortex and deep nuclei: the ACM supplies the lateral convexity (motor and sensory areas of the face and arm, Broca’s and Wernicke’s areas); the ACA supplies the medial surface (leg); the ACP supplies the occipital lobe.
MIDDLE_CEREBRAL_ARTERY.clinical: Most common site of ischaemic stroke: occlusion of the middle cerebral artery causes contralateral hemiplegia/faciobrachial hemihypoaesthesia, deviation of the gaze towards the lesion, and aphasia (if on the left) or hemineglect (if on the right).
functions: Middle Cerebral Artery (MCA): supplies 2/3 of the dorsolateral surface of the frontal, parietal and temporal lobes and the insula, plus the lenticulostriate arteries
Anterior Cerebral Artery (ACA): supplies the medial frontal and parietal regions (motor and sensory areas for the lower limb)
Posterior Cerebral Artery (PCA): supplies the visual calcarine cortex (occipital lobe), the splenium of the corpus callosum and the inferior temporal region

DURAL_VENOUS_SINUSES.name: Venous Sinuses of the Dura Mater & Internal Jugular Veins
DURAL_VENOUS_SINUSES.summary: Endothelial venous channels, devoid of valves, carved out between the periosteal and meningeal layers of the dura mater, which are responsible for draining all venous blood from the brain and the reabsorbed cerebrospinal fluid into the internal jugular veins.
DURAL_VENOUS_SINUSES.clinical: Cerebral Venous Thrombosis (CVT — refractory headache, papilloedema, seizures and haemorrhagic venous infarcts) and Septic Cavernous Sinus Thrombosis.
functions: Cortical and subcortical venous drainage to the Confluence of the Sinuses (Torcula Herophili), Transverse Sinuses and Sigmoid Sinuses
Continuous reabsorption of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) via Pacchioni’s arachnoid granulations in the superior sagittal sinus
Regulation of intracranial venous pressure (Monro–Kellie’s theory)

LATERAL_VENTRICLES.name: Lateral Ventricles & Choroid Plexuses
LATERAL_VENTRICLES.badge: VENTRICULAR SYSTEM • PRODUCTION OF CEREBROSPINAL FLUID (CSF)
LATERAL_VENTRICLES.summary: A pair of large, ‘C’-shaped ependymal cavities within each cerebral hemisphere, housing the choroid plexuses which filter plasma to produce ~500 mL of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) per day.
LATERAL_VENTRICLES.clinical: Communicating or non-communicating hydrocephalus (ventriculomegaly), normal-pressure hydrocephalus in the elderly (Hakim-Adams triad: apraxic gait, urinary incontinence and cognitive decline).
functions: Active production of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) by specialised ependymocytes in the choroid plexuses
Drainage of cerebrospinal fluid into the third ventricle via the Monro foramina
Mechanical-hydraulic damping of the brain and metabolic clearance (the glymphatic system during deep sleep)

THIRD_FOURTH_VENTRICLES.name: Third Ventricle, Aqueduct of Sylvius & Fourth Ventricle
THIRD_FOURTH_VENTRICLES.summary: The main route of cerebrospinal fluid flow through the diencephalon (3rd ventricle), it descends through the narrow Aqueduct of Sylvius in the midbrain to the fourth ventricle (between the pons/medulla and the cerebellum), exiting through the foramina of Luschka and Magendie.
THIRD_FOURTH_VENTRICLES.clinical: Acute obstructive hydrocephalus caused by stenosis of the aqueduct of Sylvius or compression of the fourth ventricle by tumours of the posterior fossa (medulloblastoma, ependymoma) and Arnold-Chiari malformation.
functions: Pulsatile unidirectional flow of cerebrospinal fluid driven by choroidal arterial systole and ependymal cilia
Passage of cerebrospinal fluid from the fourth ventricle into the subarachnoid space and the cisterna magna via the foramina of Magendie (medial) and Luschka (lateral)
Chemical communication with the circumventricular organs (Area Postrema, OVLT and Subfornical Organ)

BROCA_AREA_BA44_45.name: Broca’s Area (Lower Frontal Gyrus — Pars Opercularis & Triangularis)
BROCA_AREA_BA44_45.summary: The cortical motor centre for speech is situated in the opercular (BA 44) and triangular (BA 45) portions of the inferior frontal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere (usually the left, ~95 per cent of right-handers). It coordinates phonological planning, syntactic and grammatical structuring, and articulatory motor programming before sending commands to the primary orofacial motor cortex (Area 4).
BROCA_AREA_BA44_45.clinical: Broca’s aphasia (expressive or non-fluent aphasia due to occlusion of the superior branch (M2) of the left middle cerebral artery): telegraphic speech, agrammatism, marked articulatory effort and impaired repetition, but with largely preserved auditory comprehension and painful awareness of the deficit.
functions: Phonological coding and sequential assembly of morphemes and phonemes in articulated words (Pars Opercularis — BA 44)
Complex syntactic-grammatical processing and executive lexical-semantic selection (Pars Triangularis — BA 45)
Direct coordination with the motor cortex of the larynx, tongue, lips and palate (Inferior Precentral Gyrus) and with the Anterior Insula (Dronkers’ Gyrus)
Bidirectional integration with Wernicke’s area (BA 22) via the arcuate fasciculus and the superior longitudinal fasciculus

WERNICKE_AREA_BA22.name: Wernicke’s area (posterior superior temporal gyrus)
WERNICKE_AREA_BA22.summary: Cortical centre for phonemic decoding and lexical-semantic comprehension located in the posterior third of the left Superior Temporal Gyrus (Brodmann area 22 / Planum Temporale), adjacent to the primary auditory cortex (Heschl’s gyri — BA 41/42).
WERNICKE_AREA_BA22.clinical: Wernicke’s aphasia (receptive or fluent aphasia caused by occlusion of the inferior branch M2 of the left middle cerebral artery): fluent speech in terms of rhythm and melody (‘word salad’ / aphasic jargon), replete with phonemic paraphasias, semantic paraphasias and neologisms, accompanied by a severe inability to understand spoken or written language and anosognosia of the deficit itself.
functions: Acoustic-phonological recognition of speech sounds received from Heschl’s Transverse Circles (BA 41/42)
Access to the mental semantic lexicon: the conversion of sound sequences or graphemes into comprehensible conceptual meaning
Real-time monitoring of one’s own speech (auditory-verbal feedback) to prevent phonemic and semantic paraphasia
Projection of decoded semantic representations to Broca’s area via the arcuate fasciculus

ARCUATE_FASCICULUS_BA39_40.name: Arcuate Fascicle & Geschwind’s Territory (Supramarginal and Angular Gyrus)
ARCUATE_FASCICULUS_BA39_40.summary: An arcuate bundle of white matter that curves round the lateral Sylvian fissure to connect Wernicke’s area (BA 22) to Broca’s area (BA 44/45), integrating with the inferior parietal lobe — the supramarginal gyrus (BA 40) and the angular gyrus (BA 39, Geschwind’s territory).
ARCUATE_FASCICULUS_BA39_40.clinical: Conduction aphasia (lesion of the arcuate fasciculus / supramarginal gyrus): preserved comprehension and fluent speech, but a severe inability to repeat heard words and phonemic paraphasias with an ‘approximation pattern’ (‘conduite d’approche’). A lesion in the dominant angular gyrus (BA 39) causes Gerstmann’s syndrome (acalculia, agraphia, digital agnosia and right-left disorientation) and alexia with agraphia.
functions: Phonological Dorsal Pathway (Arcuate Fascicle): ultra-rapid somato-auditory transmission for the faithful repetition of words and the learning of new vocabulary
Supramarginal Gyrus (BA 40): the phonological loop of verbal working memory and somatosensory integration of articulation
Angular Rotation (BA 39): a multimodal visual-auditory-tactile hub essential for reading (grapheme-phoneme conversion), writing and symbolic calculation

PREFRONTAL_DLPFC_BA9_46.name: Dorsolateral Prefrontal and Orbitofrontal Cortex (Executive Functions)
PREFRONTAL_DLPFC_BA9_46.summary: The anterior multimodal association region of the frontal lobe, which is the last to complete ontogenetic myelination in humans (~25 years). It is subdivided into the dorsolateral circuit (BA 9/46 — ‘cold’ executive functions: working memory, planning and flexibility) and the orbitofrontal/ventromedial circuit (BA 10/11/12 — ‘hot’ executive functions: emotional regulation, ethics and impulse control).
PREFRONTAL_DLPFC_BA9_46.clinical: Dorsolateral Executive Dysfunction Syndrome (executive attention deficit, perseveration on the Wisconsin test and an inability to plan) and Orbitofrontal Syndrome (‘Phineas Gage’: behavioural disinhibition, childishness/immaturity, emotional lability and acquired sociopathy).
functions: Maintenance and active manipulation of information in Working Memory (Baddeley’s central executive buffer in BA 9/46)
Top-down inhibitory control over the amygdala and the limbic system, suppressing inappropriate impulsive responses
Cognitive flexibility, set-shifting and abstract hypothetical-deductive reasoning
Value-based decision-making, cognitive empathy (Theory of Mind) and moral judgement (orbitofrontal cortex, BA 11)

PRIMARY_MOTOR_M1_BA4.name: Primary Motor Cortex M1 (Precentral Gyrus & Penfield’s Homunculus)
PRIMARY_MOTOR_M1_BA4.badge: BRODMAN AREA 4 • VOLUNTARY MOTOR FUNCTION (LAYER V)
PRIMARY_MOTOR_M1_BA4.summary: An agranular cortical band located in the pre-central gyrus, immediately anterior to the central sulcus of Rolando. It houses Betz’s giant pyramidal cells in Layer V, whose axons descend through the radiate crown and the posterior limb of the internal capsule, forming the corticospinal tract and the corticonuclear tract.
PRIMARY_MOTOR_M1_BA4.clinical: Upper Motor Neuron Syndrome (contralateral hemiparesis/hemiplegia, scissors-like spasticity, deep tendon hyperreflexia, clonus and a positive Babinski sign), focal motor epileptic seizures with Jacksonian march and selective degeneration in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).
functions: Inverted and disproportionate somatotopic representation of the human body (Penfield’s motor homunculus: hand/thumb and face/tongue in the lateral convexity supplied by the ACM; leg/foot in the medial paracentral lobe supplied by the ACA)
Encoding of the force, direction and velocity of fine distal voluntary muscle contractions (particularly finger pinch and facial expressions/speech)
Direct projection from the upper motor neurons of Layer V to the alpha motor neurons of the contralateral spinal cord

PRIMARY_SOMATOSENSORY_S1_BA312.name: Primary Somatosensory Cortex S1 (Postcentral Gyrus)
PRIMARY_SOMATOSENSORY_S1_BA312.summary: A granular cortical band (coniocortex with a hyperdeveloped Layer IV) situated in the postcentral gyrus, posterior to the central sulcus of Rolando. It receives thalamic projections from the VPL nuclei (body: dorsal columns/medial lemniscus and spinothalamic tract) and the VPM nuclei (face and oral cavity via the trigeminal lemniscus).
PRIMARY_SOMATOSENSORY_S1_BA312.clinical: Hemi-hypoaesthesia or contralateral hemianaesthesia, loss of conscious proprioception (sensory ataxia), astereognosia (inability to identify objects by touch whilst blindfolded), agraphesthesia and phantom limb phenomenon due to somatotopic plastic reorganisation.
functions: Area 3a: reception of conscious proprioceptive input from neuromuscular spindles and Golgi tendon organs
Area 3b and Area 1: epicritic tactile discrimination of two points, texture and skin vibration (Meissner’s, Merkel’s and Pacini’s corpuscles)
Area 2: tactile-proprioceptive integration of the three-dimensional shape and size of objects being touched (stereognosis)
Somatotopic mapping of Penfield’s sensory homunculus (lips, tongue and fingertips with maximum cortical density)

PRIMARY_AUDITORY_A1_BA41_42.name: Primary Auditory Cortex A1 (Heschl’s Transverse Gyrus)
PRIMARY_AUDITORY_A1_BA41_42.summary: Located on the upper wall of the superior temporal gyrus (supratemporal plane), hidden deep within the lateral fissure of Sylvius. It receives acoustic signals from the medial geniculate body of the thalamus, preserving the tonotopic map of the basilar membrane of the cochlea.
PRIMARY_AUDITORY_A1_BA41_42.clinical: As each primary auditory cortex receives bilateral afferents from both ears (via the trapezoid body and the lateral lemniscus), unilateral lesions cause only a subtle difficulty in localising sound; bilateral lesions in Heschl’s gyri result in cortical deafness or pure verbal auditory agnosia.
functions: Precise tonotopic organisation: high-frequency sounds are processed in the posteromedial region and low-frequency sounds in the anterolateral region
Temporal analysis of rapid acoustic transients essential for distinguishing plosive consonants in speech
Binaural localisation of the sound source in the horizontal plane using the interaural differences in time and intensity
Immediate transmission to Wernicke’s area (BA 22) for the phonological decoding of language

PRIMARY_VISUAL_V1_BA17.name: Primary Visual Cortex V1 (Calcarine Cortex / Stria of Gennari)
PRIMARY_VISUAL_V1_BA17.summary: Situated on the upper (cuneus) and lower (lingual gyrus) margins of the calcarine sulcus on the medial surface of the occipital lobe. It is called the striated cortex because of the prominent myelinated band visible to the naked eye in Layer IVb (Gennari’s stria), which receives Gratiolet’s optic radiations from the lateral geniculate body (LGB).
PRIMARY_VISUAL_V1_BA17.clinical: Contralateral Homonymous Hemianopsia with Macular Preservation (posterior cerebral artery occlusion), Superior quadrantopsia (‘Pie in the Sky’ — lesion of the temporal Meyer loop) or inferior quadrantopsia (‘Pie on the Floor’ — lesion of the parietal radiation) and cortical blindness with Anton’s syndrome.
functions: Retinotopic map with foveal magnification: the macula (high-acuity central vision) occupies the posterior third of the occipital pole; the upper visual quadrant is projected onto the inferior calcarine lip and the lower quadrant onto the superior lip
Ocular dominance columns and orientation columns (Hubel & Wiesel: simple, complex and hypercomplex cells)
Primary feature extraction of edge orientation, spatial frequency, luminance contrast, colour (cytochrome oxidase blobs) and binocular disparity
Distribution to the occipitoparietal dorsal pathway (‘Where/How to act’) and the occipitotemporal ventral pathway (‘What it is’)

NEURON_SOMA.name: Cell Body (Soma / Pericaryon)
NEURON_SOMA.summary: Trophic and genomic centre of the pyramidal neuron in neocortical Layer V. It contains a spherical euchromatic nucleus, dense Nissl bodies (hyperactive rough endoplasmic reticulum) and a highly active Golgi complex.
NEURON_SOMA.clinical: Soma degeneration with central chromatolysis is the classic marker of retrograde axotomy and apoptosis in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and acute cerebral ischaemia.

NEURON_NUCLEUS.name: Euchromatic Nucleus & Nucleolus
NEURON_NUCLEUS.summary: A vesicular core with a predominance of decondensed euchromatin, reflecting a continuous rate of transcription of ion channels, postsynaptic receptors and tubulins for axonal maintenance.
NEURON_NUCLEUS.clinical: Abnormal intranuclear inclusions (TDP-43 in ALS/frontotemporal dementia, polyQ tail in Huntington’s disease) hijack the splicing machinery and lead to neuronal transcriptional failure.

NEURON_DENDRITES.name: Dendritic Tree & Thorns
NEURON_DENDRITES.summary: A branched tree with a long, ascending apical dendrite and basal dendrites. Covered by thousands of dendritic spines richly endowed with AMPA and NMDA glutamatergic receptors.
NEURON_DENDRITES.clinical: Early loss of dendritic spines induced by soluble β-amyloid (Aβ42) oligomers in Alzheimer’s disease; the basis of the deficit in synaptic plasticity and the failure of long-term potentiation (LTP).

NEURON_AXON_HILLOCK.name: Implantation Cone & Trigger Zone (AIS)
NEURON_AXON_HILLOCK.summary: Axon initial segment (AIS). It has the highest density of voltage-gated sodium channels (NaV1.6), acting as the digital summing device and electrical trigger for the action potential.
NEURON_AXON_HILLOCK.clinical: Channelopathies involving mutations in NaV channels (the SCN1A gene in Dravet syndrome) destabilise the firing threshold, leading to hyperexcitability and drug-resistant epileptic seizures.

NEURON_MYELIN.name: Myelin Sheath (Oligodendrocytes)
NEURON_MYELIN.summary: Multiple concentric layers of plasma membrane rich in sphingomyelin and cerebrosides, formed by oligodendrocytes in the CNS. This reduces membrane capacitance and increases transmembrane resistance.
NEURON_MYELIN.clinical: T-cell-mediated autoimmune attack against myelin basic protein (MBP) and MOG in multiple sclerosis; this causes disruption of saltatory conduction, axonal slowing and multifocal neurological deficits.

NEURON_SCHWANN.name: Schwann cell (SNP myelination)
NEURON_SCHWANN.badge: Support and Regeneration in the Nervous System
NEURON_SCHWANN.summary: A peripheral glial cell responsible for the formation of myelin on PNS axons (one myelin sheath per cell) and the secretion of neurotrophins (NGF, BDNF) during the regenerative process.
NEURON_SCHWANN.clinical: Inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (Guillain-Barré syndrome) attacks the peripheral myelin and Schwann cells following infections, triggering ascending flaccid tetraparesis with loss of reflexes.

NEURON_NODE_RANVIER.name: Ranvier’s nodes
NEURON_NODE_RANVIER.badge: Bound Propagation and Channels in NaV1.6
NEURON_NODE_RANVIER.summary: Periodic discontinuities (1–2 µm) between myelinated internodes. These contain an extremely high density of NaV1.6 channels anchored by ankyrin-G, enabling the action potential to propagate at speeds of up to 120 m/s.
NEURON_NODE_RANVIER.clinical: Anti-neurofascin 155/186 or anti-contactin antibodies attack the paranodal junction in autoimmune nodopathic neuropathies, disrupting nodal insulation and causing acute motor conduction block.

NEURON_TERMINAL.name: Terminal & Axonal Termination Button
NEURON_TERMINAL.summary: Terminal axon swelling containing abundant mitochondria, SNARE complexes (synaptobrevin, syntaxin, SNAP-25) and P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels (CaV2.1).
NEURON_TERMINAL.clinical: Bacterial toxins (botulinum toxin, tetanus) irreversibly cleave SNARE proteins, blocking the exocytosis of acetylcholine or GABA and causing fulminant flaccid or spastic paralysis.

NEURON_SYNAPSE.name: Synaptic Cleft & Postsynaptic Density
NEURON_SYNAPSE.summary: A 20 nm extracellular space between the pre- and postsynaptic membranes. The calcium influx triggers the release of glutamate into the synaptic cleft, where it binds to AMPA, NMDA and mGluR receptors on the postsynaptic density (PSD-95).
NEURON_SYNAPSE.clinical: Overexposure to glutamate during acute ischaemia causes a massive, uncontrolled influx of calcium via hyperactivated NMDA receptors, leading to excitotoxicity, mitochondrial dysfunction and a cascade of apoptosis.

MENINGES_DURA_ARACHNOID_PIA.name: Meninges (duramadre, aracnoides y piamadre)
MENINGES_DURA_ARACHNOID_PIA.badge: MENINGES Y SEPTOS DURALES • PROTECCIÓN DEL SNC
MENINGES_DURA_ARACHNOID_PIA.summary: Tres membranas concéntricas que recubren y protegen el sistema nervioso central: (1) la duramadre (paquimeninge fibrosa externa con la hoz cerebral en la fisura interhemisférica y el tentorio del cerebelo), (2) membrana aracnoidea trabecular en el espacio subaracnoideo, relleno de líquido cefalorraquídeo (LCR), y las granulaciones aracnoideas de Pacchioni junto al seno sagital superior, y (3) piamadre vascular íntima adherida a las circunvoluciones y surcos corticales.
MENINGES_DURA_ARACHNOID_PIA.clinical: Meningitis bacteriana o viral (rigidez de la nuca, signos de Kernig y Brudzinski), hematoma epidural (rotura de la arteria meníngea media), hematoma subdural (rotura de las venas puente corticales) y hemorragia subaracnoidea.
functions: Protección mecánica contra traumatismos craneoencefálicos y compartimentación craneal (hoz cerebral y tentorio del cerebelo)
Soporte hidrostático del cerebro flotante en el líquido cefalorraquídeo (lo que reduce el peso efectivo de 1.400 g a unos 50 g)
Reabsorción unidireccional del líquido cefalorraquídeo (LCR) a través de las granulaciones aracnoideas de Pacchioni hacia el seno sagital superior
Barrera hematoliquórica y revestimiento pial perivascular (espacios de Virchow-Robin / sistema glinfático)

FRONTAL_LOBE.name: Lobo Frontal
FRONTAL_LOBE.summary: Sede de las funciones ejecutivas superiores, la planificación, el control inhibitorio (corteza prefrontal dorsolateral y orbitofrontal), la motricidad voluntaria somatotópica (giro precentral / homúnculo motor de Penfield) y la expresión motora del habla (área de Broca).
FRONTAL_LOBE.clinical: Afasia motora de Broca (habla no fluida con comprensión intacta), hemiparesia/hemiplejía contralateral, síndrome de ejecución deficiente o apatía/desinhibición frontal (síndrome de Phineas Gage) y demencia frontotemporal.
functions: Ejecución motora voluntaria contralateral a través del tracto corticoespinal piramidal (área 4)
Planificación motora compleja, coordinación bimanual y visión conjunta (Áreas 6 y 8)
Memoria de trabajo, abstracción, juicio ético y regulación de la conducta social (Áreas 9–12)
Programación fonológica y sintáctica del lenguaje hablado y escrito (Área de Broca — 44 y 45)

PARIETAL_LOBE.name: Lobo parietal
PARIETAL_LOBE.summary: Centro primario de integración somatosensorial (tacto epicrítico, propiocepción consciente, dolor y temperatura en el giro poscentral), percepción visoespacial, esquema corporal y cálculo simbólico.
PARIETAL_LOBE.clinical: Negligencia espacial contralateral (lesión parietal derecha), astereognosia, apraxia ideomotora y síndrome de Gerstmann (agnosia digital, acalculia, agrafía y desorientación derecha-izquierda en el giro angular dominante).
functions: Somatotopía sensorial primaria en el giro poscentral (homúnculo sensorial — áreas 3, 1 y 2)
Estereognosia (reconocimiento táctil de objetos) y grafestesia en el lóbulo parietal superior
Integración semántica multimodal, lectura y cálculo en los giros supramarginal (40) y angular (39)
Atención espacial tridimensional y mapa egocéntrico/alocéntrico del espacio peripersonal

TEMPORAL_LOBE.name: Lobo Temporal
TEMPORAL_LOBE.summary: Procesa la audición primaria (giros transversales de Heschl), la comprensión semántica del lenguaje (área de Wernicke), el reconocimiento visual de rostros (giro fusiforme) y alberga en su cara medial el complejo hipocampo-amígdala.
TEMPORAL_LOBE.clinical: Afasia sensorial de Wernicke (habla fluida, aunque parafrásica o neológica, y sin comprensión), prosopagnosia (incapacidad para reconocer rostros) y epilepsia del lóbulo temporal con auras olfativas y déjà vu.
functions: Tonotopía auditiva primaria y secundaria en los giros de Heschl (áreas 41 y 42)
Decodificación fonémica y comprensión del lenguaje en el área de Wernicke (área 22 posterior)
Vía visual ventral («¿Qué?»): reconocimiento de objetos y rostros en el giro fusiforme (área 37)
Integración auditivo-límbica y consolidación de los recuerdos semánticos a largo plazo

OCCIPITAL_LOBE.name: Lobo occipital
OCCIPITAL_LOBE.summary: Dedicado íntegramente a la visión, recibe las proyecciones ópticas del cuerpo geniculado lateral en los bordes del surco calcáreo (V1 / Área 17 — Estría de Gennari) y las distribuye a las áreas asociativas V2–V5.
OCCIPITAL_LOBE.clinical: Hemianopsia homónima contralateral con preservación macular (oclusión de la arteria cerebral posterior), ceguera cortical con síndrome de Anton (negación de la ceguera y confabulación visual) y acromatopsia central.
functions: Correspondencia retinotópica punto a punto en la corteza visual primaria (V1 / Área 17)
Descomposición de la orientación de los bordes, contraste binocular, disparidad de profundidad y color (V2/V4)
Percepción del movimiento y velocidad óptica (Área V5 / MT)
Origen de las vías visuales dorsal (parietal — «Dónde/Cómo actuar») y ventral (temporal — «Qué es»)

INSULAR_CORTEX.name: Corteza insular (ínsula de Reil)
INSULAR_CORTEX.summary: Quinto lóbulo cerebral oculto en el fondo del surco lateral de Sylvius, responsable de la interocepción consciente (percepción de los latidos del corazón, la respiración, el dolor visceral y el hambre), el gusto primario y la empatía afectiva.
INSULAR_CORTEX.clinical: Arritmias neurogénicas e inversión de la onda T tras un ictus insular derecho, pérdida repentina de la fisura por nicotina o dependencia química tras una lesión insular y alteraciones en la percepción del dolor (asimbolia del dolor).
functions: Mapa interoceptivo visceral consciente (estado fisiológico interno del cuerpo)
Corteza gustativa primaria e integración olfativo-gustativa del paladar
Procesamiento de la matriz afectiva del dolor, aversión al riesgo, asco y empatía emocional
Control autonómico cardiovascular (modulación simpática/parasimpática de la frecuencia cardíaca)

CEREBELLUM.name: Cerebelo (folia, vermis y hemisferios)
CEREBELLUM.summary: Contiene más de la mitad de todas las neuronas del cerebro humano (~69 mil millones), organizadas en finas láminas horizontales (folia) y células de Purkinje que comparan la intención motora cortical con la retroalimentación propioceptiva en tiempo real.
CEREBELLUM.clinical: Síndrome cerebeloso ipsilateral: ataxia de la marcha (base ensanchada), dismetría (prueba del índice a la nariz), disdiadococinesia, temblor intencional, disartria escandida y nistagmo.
functions: Coordinación fina de la fuerza, la amplitud y la sincronización muscular (metría y diadococinesia)
Mantenimiento del equilibrio axial y del reflejo vestíbulo-ocular (lóbulo floculonodular y vermis)
Corrección instantánea de errores motores a través de las fibras trepadoras de la amígdala inferior sobre las células de Purkinje
Aprendizaje motor procedimental y automatización de habilidades cognitivo-motoras

CORPUS_CALLOSUM.name: Cuerpo liso
CORPUS_CALLOSUM.summary: La estructura de sustancia blanca más grande del sistema nervioso (~200 millones de axones mielinizados), que conecta de forma homotópica y heterotópica los hemisferios cerebrales izquierdo y derecho.
CORPUS_CALLOSUM.clinical: Síndrome de desconexión interhemisférica (cerebro dividido), síndrome de la mano ajena (Alien Hand Syndrome), alexia sin agrafía (lesión del esplenio y de la corteza occipital izquierda) y agenesia del cuerpo calloso.
functions: Transferencia interhemisférica ultrarrápida de información sensorial, motora y lingüística
Unificación de los campos visuales izquierdo y derecho a través del esplenio del cuerpo calloso
Coordinación motora bimanual sincronizada a través de la rodilla y el cuerpo calloso
Integración de la prosodia emocional (hemisferio derecho) con la sintaxis verbal (hemisferio izquierdo)

THALAMUS.name: Tálamo (diencéfalo dorsal)
THALAMUS.summary: Estación de retransmisión y filtrado obligatoria para todas las vías sensoriales conscientes (excepto el olfato), además de integrar los circuitos motores de los núcleos basales y del cerebelo hacia la corteza cerebral.
THALAMUS.clinical: Síndrome de dolor talámico de Dejerine-Roussy (hemihipoestesia seguida de dolor neuropático alodínico insoportable contralateral tras un ictus talámico posterolateral) e insomnio familiar mortal.
functions: Transmisión somatosensorial del cuerpo (núcleo VPL) y de la cara/trigémino (núcleo VPM)
Transmisión visual (cuerpo geniculado lateral — CGL) y auditiva (cuerpo geniculado medial — CGM)
Modulación de los circuitos motores de los núcleos de la base del cerebro y el cerebelo (núcleos ventral anterior y ventral lateral)
Regulación del ciclo vigilia-sueño y de los ritmos alfa y de hilos del sueño por parte del núcleo reticular talámico

HYPOTHALAMUS.name: Hipotálamo y eje hipofisario
HYPOTHALAMUS.summary: Maestro supremo de la homeostasis corporal y del sistema nervioso autónomo, vinculado a la hipófisis (glándula pituitaria) para traducir las señales neuronales en control hormonal sistémico.
HYPOTHALAMUS.clinical: Diabetes insípida central (deficiencia de ADH), síndrome de secreción inadecuada de ADH (SIADH), narcolepsia (pérdida de neuronas orexinérgicas) y trastornos graves de la termorregulación.
functions: Termorregulación (el hipotálamo anterior disipa el calor; el posterior lo conserva)
Reloj biológico endógeno circadiano de 24 horas en el núcleo supraquiasmático
Control de la sed/osmolaridad, el hambre/la saciedad (núcleos arqueado, ventromedial y lateral)
Síntesis de oxitocina y ADH (vasopresina) en los núcleos supraóptico y paraventricular y control de la adenohipófisis

HIPPOCAMPUS.name: Hipocampo y fórnix
HIPPOCAMPUS.summary: El arcocórtex temporal medial es esencial para la consolidación de la memoria declarativa (episódica y semántica) y para la cartografía espacial cognitiva (células de lugar / place cells).
HIPPOCAMPUS.clinical: Amnesia anterógrada grave (incapacidad para formar nuevos recuerdos declarativos, como en el caso del clásico paciente H.M.), atrofia hipocampal precoz en la enfermedad de Alzheimer y la esclerosis mesial temporal.
functions: Consolidación sináptica de los recuerdos a corto plazo en recuerdos a largo plazo mediante la potenciación de larga duración (LTP)
Circuito trisináptico del hipocampo (corteza entorrinal → giro dentado → CA3 → CA1 → subículo → fórnix)
Navegación espacial y orientación geográfica mediante las «células de lugar» (hipocampo) y las «células de rejilla» (corteza entorrinal)
Neurogénesis adulta continua en la zona subgranular del giro dentado

AMYGDALA.name: Amígdala cerebral (complejo amigdaliano)
AMYGDALA.summary: Vigilante emocional del sistema límbico situado en el polo temporal anterior, que atribuye una valencia afectiva inmediata a los estímulos sensoriales y desencadena la respuesta autonómica de lucha o huida.
AMYGDALA.clinical: Trastorno por estrés postraumático (TEPT), trastornos de ansiedad/pánico (hiperreactividad amigdalar con hipofunción prefrontal) y síndrome de Klüver-Bucy (placidez, hiperoralidad y ausencia de miedo tras una lesión bilateral).
functions: Condicionamiento al miedo y detección ultrarrápida de amenazas ambientales (a través de la vía talámico-amigdaliana)
Modulación emocional de la consolidación de los recuerdos en el hipocampo (recuerdos emocionalmente intensos)
Activación autonómica simpática y neuroendocrina (eje HPA / cortisol) a través del núcleo central de la amígdala
Reconocimiento de expresiones faciales de miedo, ira y confianza social

BASAL_GANGLIA.name: Núcleos de la base (cuerpo estriado y globo pálido)
BASAL_GANGLIA.badge: SELECCIÓN DE ACCIONAMIENTOS Y AUTOMATIZACIÓN DE MOTORES
BASAL_GANGLIA.summary: Complejo de núcleos subcorticales profundos que actúan en los circuitos cortico-estriado-pálido-talámico-corticales (vía directa facilitadora y vía indirecta inhibitoria) para iniciar los movimientos deseados y suprimir los movimientos parásitos.
BASAL_GANGLIA.clinical: Enfermedad de Parkinson (degeneración dopaminérgica de la sustancia negra → bradicinesia, rigidez en forma de rueda dentada y temblor en reposo), corea de Huntington y hemibalismo (lesión del núcleo subtalámico de Luys).
functions: Vía directa (receptores D1): desinhibe el tálamo y facilita el inicio fluido de los movimientos voluntarios
Vía indirecta (receptores D2): inhibe el tálamo para suprimir los movimientos involuntarios no deseados
Modulación dopaminérgica nigroestriatal procedente de la sustancia negra pars compacta (SNpc)
Aprendizaje por refuerzo, formación de hábitos y motivación (estrado ventral / núcleo accumbens)

MIDBRAIN.name: Mesencéfalo (tronco encefálico superior)
MIDBRAIN.summary: Segmento superior del tronco encefálico atravesado por el acueducto cerebral de Sylvius, que contiene los pedúnculos cerebrales, los colículos superior e inferior, el núcleo rubro, la sustancia negra y el área tegmental ventral (VTA).
MIDBRAIN.clinical: Síndrome de Weber (hemiplejía contralateral + parálisis del III par ipsilateral con ptosis y midriasis), síndrome de Parinaud (parálisis del movimiento ocular conjugado vertical superior) y rigidez descerebrada.
functions: Orientación refleja de la cabeza y los ojos ante estímulos visuales (colículos superiores) y sonoros (colículos inferiores)
Origen de los nervios oculomotor (NC III — motricidad ocular y reflejo fotomotor pupilar de Edinger-Westphal) y troclear (NC IV)
Producción de dopamina en la sustancia negra (vía nigroestriatal) y en la VTA (vías mesolímbica y mesocortical)
Analgesia endógena descendente a través de la sustancia gris periacueductal (PAG)

PONS.name: Puente de Varolio (protuberancia anular)
PONS.summary: Protuberancia ventral del tronco encefálico situada entre el mesencéfalo y el bulbo, que actúa como un gran puente de fibras transversales entre la corteza cerebral y el cerebelo y que alberga los núcleos de los nervios V, VI, VII y VIII.
PONS.clinical: Síndrome de cautiverio / síndrome de «locked-in» (infarto ventral de la base del puente por oclusión basilar -> tetraplejia y anartria con conciencia intacta y movimiento ocular vertical conservado) y mielinólisis pontina central.
functions: Transmisión masiva de comandos corticales al cerebelo a través de los núcleos pontinos y el pedúnculo cerebeloso medio
Centros neumotáxico y apneústico (regulación precisa de la transición entre la inspiración y la espiración)
Núcleos de los nervios trigémino (CN V), abducente (CN VI), facial (CN VII) y vestibulococlear (CN VIII)
La principal fuente de noradrenalina para todo el cerebro se encuentra en el locus coeruleus (vigilancia y atención)

MEDULLA_OBLONGATA.name: Bulbo raquídeo (médula oblonga)
MEDULLA_OBLONGATA.summary: Segmento caudal del tronco encefálico, que se une a la médula espinal en el foramen magnum, y que contiene la decusación de las pirámides (cruce motor del 85 % de las fibras corticoespinales) y los centros vitales autónomos.
MEDULLA_OBLONGATA.clinical: Síndrome bulbar lateral de Wallenberg (oclusión de la PICA → disfagia, ronquera, síndrome de Horner ipsilateral, vértigo y pérdida termoalgésica cruzada) y paro cardiorrespiratorio en una hernia amigdalar.
functions: Control automático de la generación del ritmo respiratorio (grupos respiratorios dorsal y ventral / complejo de Pre-Bötzinger)
Regulación latido a latido de la presión arterial y la frecuencia cardíaca (núcleo del tracto solitario y bulbo rostroventrolateral)
Decusación motora de las pirámides (tracto corticoespinal lateral) y decusación sensitiva del lemnisco medial (grácil y cuneiforme)
Núcleos de los nervios glosofaríngeo (IX), vago (X), accesorio (XI) e hipogloso (XII): deglución, fonación, tos y vómito

SPINAL_CORD.name: Médula espinal, cono medular y cola de caballo
SPINAL_CORD.badge: SISTEMA NERVIOSO CENTRAL • VÍAS MOTORAS Y SENSORIALES
SPINAL_CORD.summary: Eje cilíndrico del sistema nervioso central protegido por el canal vertebral, en el que se aprecia la médula espinal de sustancia gris (cuernos dorsal sensitivo, intermedio autónomo y ventral motor) rodeado por los funículos de sustancia blanca y que termina en el cono medular (L1/L2) y la cola de caballo.
SPINAL_CORD.clinical: Síndrome de hemisección medular de Brown-Séquard (parálisis y pérdida propioceptiva ipsilateral + pérdida termoalgésica contralateral), síndrome de la cola de caballo (anestesia en silla de montar y retención urinaria) y esclerosis lateral amiotrófica (ELA).
functions: Conducción motora descendente a través de las vías corticoespinales lateral y anterior, rubroespinal, retículoespinal y vestibuloespinal
Conducción sensitiva ascendente a través de las columnas dorsales (nervios gracilis y cuneiforme: tacto epicrítico y propiocepción) y del tracto espinotalámico (dolor y temperatura)
Integración de los arcos reflejos medulares (reflejo miotático rotuliano/aquileo y reflejo flexor de retirada)
Origen de la columna simpática toracolumbar (T1–L2) y parasimpática sacra (S2–S4), así como de las raíces de la cola de caballo

OLFACTORY_NERVE_CN1.name: Nervio olfativo (I par craneal)
OLFACTORY_NERVE_CN1.badge: I PAR CRANÍACO • EL OLFATO LLEGA DIRECTAMENTE A LA CORTEZA CEREBRAL
OLFACTORY_NERVE_CN1.summary: Primer par craneal, puramente sensorial especial (aferente visceral especial), y la única vía sensorial humana que llega directamente a la corteza olfativa primaria (piriforme y amígdala) sin pasar antes por el tálamo.
OLFACTORY_NERVE_CN1.clinical: Anosmia o hiposmia postraumática (fractura de la lámina cribiforme con fístula liquórica / rinorrea de LCR), hiposmia prodrómica temprana en la enfermedad de Parkinson y el síndrome de Foster-Kennedy.
functions: Transducción química de moléculas odoríferas por los cilios de las neuronas bipolares de la mucosa olfativa superior
Recorrido de los filamentos olfativos a través de los orificios de la lámina cribosa del hueso etmoides hasta los glomérulos del bulbo olfativo
Conexión directa con la corteza piriforme, la amígdala y la corteza entorrinal (evocación instantánea de recuerdos afectivos a través del olfato)

OPTIC_NERVE_CN2.name: Nervio óptico, quiasma y tracto óptico (II par)
OPTIC_NERVE_CN2.summary: Está formado por los axones de las células ganglionares de la retina (mielinizados por oligodendrocitos, lo que lo convierte en un verdadero tracto del diencéfalo), cuyas fibras nasales se cruzan en el quiasma óptico de camino al cuerpo geniculado lateral.
OPTIC_NERVE_CN2.clinical: Neuritis óptica retrobulbar (a menudo manifestación inicial de la esclerosis múltiple, con defecto pupilar aferente relativo de Marcus Gunn), hemianopsia bitemporal heterónima (compresión del quiasma por un adenoma hipofisario) y papiledema.
functions: Imágenes de alta resolución de la retina foveal (mácula) y periférica
Decusación de las fibras de la hemirretina nasal en el quiasma óptico (que une los hemicampos visuales izquierdo y derecho)
Evaluación del reflejo fotomotor pupilar directo y consensual hacia el área pretectal del mesencéfalo

OCULOMOTOR_NERVES_CN3_4_6.name: Nervios oculomotor (III), troclear (IV) y abducente (VI)
OCULOMOTOR_NERVES_CN3_4_6.badge: PARES III, IV y VI • MOTRICIDAD OCULAR EXTRÍNSECA E INTRÍNSECA
OCULOMOTOR_NERVES_CN3_4_6.summary: Trío de nervios craneales motores que atraviesan el seno cavernoso y la fisura orbitaria superior para controlar con precisión micrométrica los seis músculos extraoculares, el elevador del párpado y el esfínter de la pupila.
OCULOMOTOR_NERVES_CN3_4_6.clinical: Parálisis del III par (desviación del ojo hacia fuera y hacia abajo, ptosis palpebral y midriasis fija por aneurisma de la arteria comunicante posterior), diplopía vertical al bajar escaleras (lesión del IV par) y estrabismo convergente (lesión del VI par).
functions: CN III (oculomotora): inerva el recto superior, el recto inferior, el recto medial, el oblicuo inferior, el elevador del párpado y la miosis pupilar (Edinger-Westphal)
CN IV (Troclear): único nervio que emerge de la cara dorsal del tronco y que inerva el músculo oblicuo superior (intorsión y depresión del ojo)
CN VI (abductora): inerva el músculo recto lateral, lo que permite la abducción horizontal del globo ocular

TRIGEMINAL_NERVE_CN5.name: Nervio trigémino (V Par: ramas V1, V2 y V3)
TRIGEMINAL_NERVE_CN5.badge: V PAR CRANÍACO • SENSIBILIDAD FACIAL Y MASTICACIÓN
TRIGEMINAL_NERVE_CN5.summary: El más grueso de los nervios craneales, que emerge de la cara anterolateral del puente y se ramifica en el ganglio trigémino (semilunar de Gasser) en tres ramas principales: oftálmico (V1), maxilar (V2) y mandibular (V3).
TRIGEMINAL_NERVE_CN5.clinical: Neuralgia del trigémino (ataques de dolor punzante similar a una descarga eléctrica en los territorios V2/V3, a menudo debidos a una compresión neurovascular por parte de la arteria cerebelosa superior), fisiopatología de la migraña (sistema trigémino-vascular) y herpes zóster oftálmico.
functions: Sensibilidad táctil, térmica y al dolor en toda la cara, la córnea, los senos paranasales, los dientes, la parte anterior de la lengua (2/3) y la duramadre
Inervación motora branquial (rama V3) de los músculos masticatorios (masetero, temporal, pterigoideos medial y lateral)
Evaluación del reflejo corneopalpebral (V1) y del reflejo mentoniano/massetérico (V3)

FACIAL_VESTIBULOCOCHLEAR_CN7_8.name: Nervios facial (VII) y vestibulococlear (VIII)
FACIAL_VESTIBULOCOCHLEAR_CN7_8.badge: VII y VIII PARES • MÍMICA FACIAL, AUDICIÓN Y EQUILIBRIO
FACIAL_VESTIBULOCOCHLEAR_CN7_8.summary: Salen juntos en el ángulo pontocerebeloso y penetran en el meato acústico interno: el VII par controla la mímica facial, el lagrimeo, la salivación y el gusto anterior; el VIII par se encarga de la audición (cóclea) y del equilibrio (laberinto vestibular).
FACIAL_VESTIBULOCOCHLEAR_CN7_8.clinical: Parálisis facial periférica de Bell (afecta a los planos superior e inferior de la hemifaz ipsilateral con signo de Bell), vértigo posicional paroxístico benigno (VPPB), enfermedad de Ménière y schwannoma vestibular.
functions: CN VII (facial): motricidad de todos los músculos de la expresión facial, sentido del gusto en los dos tercios anteriores de la lengua (corda del tímpano) y glándulas lacrimales, submandibulares y sublinguales
CN VIII (división coclear): transducción sonora desde el órgano de Corti hacia los núcleos cocleares
CN VIII (división vestibular): detección de la aceleración angular (canales semicirculares) y lineal (utrículo y sáculo)

VAGUS_NERVE_CN10.name: Nervio vago (X par) y eje parasimpático
VAGUS_NERVE_CN10.badge: PAR CRANÍACO X • PARASIMPÁTICO TORACOABDOMINAL PRINCIPAL
VAGUS_NERVE_CN10.summary: Es el nervio craneal de mayor longitud, que desciende por el cuello (vaina carotídea), el mediastino y el hiato esofágico para suministrar aproximadamente el 75 % de todas las fibras parasimpáticas del cuerpo humano hasta el colon transverso.
VAGUS_NERVE_CN10.clinical: Ronquera/disfonía por parálisis de la pliegue vocal (lesión del nervio laríngeo recurrente), síncope vasovagal, gastroparesia diabética y estimulación del nervio vago (VNS) para la epilepsia refractaria y la depresión resistente.
functions: Reducción de la frecuencia cardíaca (efecto cronotrópico negativo en el nódulo sinoauricular) y broncoconstricción fisiológica
Estimulación del peristaltismo gastrointestinal y de la secreción de ácido gástrico, bilis y jugos pancreáticos (eje intestino-cerebro)
Inervación motora de la laringe (nervio laríngeo recurrente — fónacion) y del paladar blando, además del reflejo barorreceptor
Vía colinérgica antiinflamatoria (modulación vagal de la respuesta inmunitaria sistémica)

GLOSSOPHARYNGEAL_ACCESSORY_HYPOGLOSSAL_C.name: Nervios glosofaríngeo (IX), accesorio (XI) e hipogloso (XII)
GLOSSOPHARYNGEAL_ACCESSORY_HYPOGLOSSAL_C.badge: PARES IX, XI Y XII • DEGLUCIÓN, FONOARTICULACIÓN Y CUELLO
GLOSSOPHARYNGEAL_ACCESSORY_HYPOGLOSSAL_C.summary: Nervios bulbares inferiores que coordinan la sensibilidad faríngea y del seno carotídeo (IX), la rotación cervical y la elevación de los hombros (XI) y la motricidad intrínseca y extrínseca de la lengua (XII).
GLOSSOPHARYNGEAL_ACCESSORY_HYPOGLOSSAL_C.clinical: Neuralgia glosofaríngea, síndrome del foramen yugular (Vernet — IX, X y XI), caída del hombro por lesión del par XI y desviación de la lengua hacia el lado de la lesión con atrofia y fasciculaciones en la lesión del par XII.
functions: CN IX (glosofaríngeo): sentido del gusto y sensibilidad del tercio posterior de la lengua, reflejo nauseoso, glándula parótida y quimio/barorreceptores del seno carotídeo
CN XI (accesorio espinal): inervación motora de los músculos esternocleidomastoideo y trapecio
CN XII (hipogloso): controla el movimiento de todos los músculos de la lengua (geniogloso, hipogloso, estilogloso)

CERVICAL_PLEXUS_PHRENIC.name: Plexo cervical y nervio frénico (C1–C5)
CERVICAL_PLEXUS_PHRENIC.summary: Formado por las ramas ventrales de C1 a C4 (con aportación de C5), da origen al ramo cervical que inerva los músculos infrahiodeos y al vital nervio frénico (C3, C4, C5), único responsable de la contracción del músculo diafragma.
CERVICAL_PLEXUS_PHRENIC.clinical: Parálisis diafragmática con elevación paradójica de la hemicúpula diafragmática (lesión del nervio frénico) o parada respiratoria mecánica en traumatismo raquimédular cervical alto (por encima de C3).
functions: Control rítmico y voluntario del diafragma a través del nervio frénico («C3, C4, C5: mantén vivo el diafragma»)
Sensibilidad cutánea del cuero cabelludo occipital, el pabellón auricular, la parte anterior del cuello y la región supraclavicular
Sensibilidad dolorosa referida del pericardio, la pleura mediastínica y el peritoneo subdiafragmático (dolor referido en el hombro — Signo de Kehr)

BRACHIAL_PLEXUS.name: Plexo braquial (raíces C5–T1, troncos y fascículos)
BRACHIAL_PLEXUS.badge: SNP DE LA EXTREMIDAD SUPERIOR • RED AXILAR
BRACHIAL_PLEXUS.summary: Compleja red anastomótica formada por las ramas anteriores de C5 a T1 que atraviesa el desfiladero interescalénico y se divide en troncos (superior, medio e inferior), divisiones y fascículos (lateral, medial y posterior) para inervar toda la extremidad superior.
BRACHIAL_PLEXUS.clinical: Parálisis de Erb-Duchenne (lesión de C5–C6 → postura en «cuello de camarero»), parálisis de Klumpke (lesión de C8–T1 → mano en garra + síndrome de Horner) y síndrome del estrecho torácico.
functions: Tronco superior (C5–C6): abducción del hombro (nervio axilar / deltoides) y flexión del codo (nervio musculocutáneo / bíceps)
Fascículo posterior: extensión de toda la extremidad superior a través del nervio radial
Fascículos lateral y medial: motricidad flexora e intrínseca fina de la mano a través de los nervios mediano y cubital

MEDIAN_ULNAR_RADIAL_NERVES.name: Nervios mediano, cubital y radial (brazo, antebrazo y mano)
MEDIAN_ULNAR_RADIAL_NERVES.badge: SNP BRAQUIAL • MOTRICIDAD FINA DE LA MANO
MEDIAN_ULNAR_RADIAL_NERVES.summary: Tríada de grandes nervios terminales del plexo braquial que recorren el brazo, el codo, el antebrazo y la muñeca (túnel carpiano y canal de Guyon) para controlar la prensión, la pinza fina y la extensión de los dedos.
MEDIAN_ULNAR_RADIAL_NERVES.clinical: Síndrome del túnel carpiano / Mano simiesca (lesión del nervio mediano), mano en garra cubital (signo de Froment en la lesión del nervio cubital) y mano caída / Wrist Drop (lesión del nervio radial en el surco espiral del húmero).
functions: Nervio mediano (C5–T1): pronación del antebrazo, oposición del pulgar (eminencia tenar) y sensibilidad palmar del 1.º al 3.º dedo
Nervio cubital (C8–T1): músculos intrínsecos de la mano (interóseos, aductor del pulgar e hipotenar) y sensibilidad del quinto dedo
Nervio radial (C5–T1): extensión del codo (tríceps), la muñeca y los dedos (compartimento posterior)

INTERCOSTAL_SYMPATHETIC_CHAIN.name: Nervios intercostales (T1–T12) y cadena simpática toracolumbar
